title: Advaita Vedānta — the self and ultimate reality are nondual
when: Advaita draws on the ancient Upaniṣads, composed over centuries in the first millennium BCE. Its early history before Gauḍapāda is difficult to reconstruct. Śaṅkara, generally placed in the eighth century CE though dates are disputed, systematized rather than founded the tradition.
people: Upaniṣadic teachers such as Yājñavalkya; Gauḍapāda, whose dates are uncertain; and Śaṅkara, whose commentaries shaped classical Advaita.
origin: The Indian subcontinent, within Vedānta’s interpretation of the Upaniṣads and Brahma Sūtras and in debate with other Indian philosophical schools.
idea: Advaita means “non-secondness.” It holds that Brahman is reality’s nondual ground and ātman—the deepest self—is not ultimately other than Brahman. Ignorance makes names, forms, and the individual self seem independently real. This does not mean the everyday ego is God or that the world is nonexistent: Śaṅkara accepts practical reality while denying its ultimacy. Through scriptural study, reasoning, and contemplation, one can recognize this identity; liberation (mokṣa) is knowledge of it, not a state newly produced.
relevance: Advaita remains a living Hindu tradition and offers a distinctive framework for debates about consciousness, personal identity, and whether a self can be understood apart from the world.
